opening.headline: When determining where to place filters to separate prompts and responses at the front end of a model, let's explore this from the perspective of Model Armor.
body: User inputs may contain mixed attempts at prompt injection or escape attempts. Personal information and internal company secrets could be embedded within prompts or responses and potentially leaked externally, or the model might generate harmful or brand-inappropriate content. Filtering each agent's code separately with dedicated filters would result in inconsistent standards.

In this lesson, we examine diagrams that illustrate how Google Cloud's Model Armor checks prompts and responses, and where this checking occurs when integrated with the Agent Gateway. We also distinguish between gateway-level filters and model-level safety settings, and explain with examples where filtering is applied in the request and response pathways.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role and application points of Model Armor.
Gateway filtering and model safety settings can be distinguished.

screens.title: Prompt and response filtering is required at the model frontend.
screens.lead: First, please read about the risks involved when directly calling a model without a filter. The diagram compares a structure where each agent has its own filter with a structure where a single filter is placed at the central hub.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing two structures: one where each agent has its own filter with different criteria, and another where a single filter is placed at a central point so all agents use the same criteria.
labels: The same standard for all agents

paragraphs: Let's assume that multiple teams are developing and operating internal AI agents. User inputs may contain prompt injection or escape attempts. Personal information or internal confidential data might be included in prompts or responses and could be exposed externally. The model might generate harmful or brand-inappropriate content.

The easiest approach is to add filters to each agent's code. However, standards vary across teams, and it's easy to forget adding filters when new agents are created. Additionally, filter behavior might change when the model is updated.

Therefore, we need a method of placing a filter at a single point along the path that requests and responses pass through. The second question of this lesson is how a filter at the junction differs from the safety settings inherent to the model itself.

callout.label: Questions to be answered in this class
callout.text: Where should the filter be placed to ensure consistent control, and how does it differ from the safety settings of the model itself?

screens.outro: First, let's directly recall the difference between the two approaches.

screens.title: Recall the difference between gateway filters and model safety settings
screens.lead: First, think through each question on your own before selecting an answer. The instructor's thoughts will then be organized and presented. No answers are submitted.

items.prompt: What does a gateway-level filter look like?
items.answer: This is a mechanism that checks and filters requests and responses as they pass through. It operates independently of the model, so the same policy is maintained even if the model or agent changes.

items.prompt: What does model-level safety configuration look like?
items.answer: This is a way of setting thresholds by hazardous category, among other model call configuration options. It is a layer that operates during the call, and the baseline may change if the model or settings change.

items.prompt: Which side will more easily enforce the same standards across the entire organization?
items.answer: A gateway filter placed at the gateway level. A policy defined at one location is applied to all agents managed by the gateway. However, it is not necessary to disable the model safety settings, and both can be used together.

items.prompt: If a filter is already in use, will changing the model still maintain the same criteria?
items.answer: If the filter is bound to the model call configuration, it may not be preserved. The stability of changes depends on whether the filter is located inside or outside the model.

screens.outro: Next, we will examine the Model Armor's inspection process using a flowchart.

screens.title: Model Armor: A service that filters prompts and responses
screens.lead: When you select the figure number marker, you can view detailed descriptions for each point in the Model Armor flow.

visual.alt: The user prompt undergoes Model Armor inspection before being passed to the model, and the model's response undergoes another Model Armor inspection before being returned to the user.
labels: Template: Filter and threshold, blocking, masking, recording only

markers.label: User prompt
markers.title: Input being tested
markers.body: Model Armor is a Google Cloud service that proactively examines the prompts and responses of large language models. The user's prompts are reviewed before they reach the model. It can be applied to AI applications both within and outside of Google Cloud.

markers.label: Input check
markers.title: Injects, extracts, and filters harmful content
markers.body: Input validation includes blocking prompt injection and escape attempts, masking and mitigating exposure of sensitive information, and filtering of harmful content. Harmful content categories include offensive language, harassment, sexual content, and dangerous content, among others, and a confidence threshold can be set for each category. Input validation can also be applied to document text and image inputs.

markers.label: LLM
markers.title: Only sanitized prompts reach the model.
markers.body: Prompts that pass validation are delivered to the LLM in a sanitized form, such as masking sensitive information if necessary. If a block detection is triggered, the model is not invoked.

markers.label: response check
markers.title: Check once more before leaving
markers.body: LLM responses are also checked in the same way before being returned to the user. The response includes detailed explanations of both activated and deactivated filters, allowing users to track why a response was blocked or why it was allowed.

markers.label: template
markers.title: Policies are defined by template.
markers.body: Defines a filter template specifying which filter to enable and what threshold value to use. It can be configured to block or mask content that violates rules, or simply to inspect and log the content. The same policy can be easily reused in multiple locations.

screens.outro: Having verified the flow of the audit service, I'll now examine where it would be applied when integrated with the gateway.

screens.title: Agent Gateway Integration: Application Points
screens.lead: Select each tab to verify where Model Armor is applied and the default behavior in the Agent Gateway.

tabs.label: Agent Gateway
tabs.body:
Agent Gateway is the entry and exit point for all interactions involving agents. It protects connections between users and agents, agents and tools, and agents and agents.

Gateway policies are composed of IAM access policies, Model Armor, and policy-based governance policies. By default, connections are blocked unless explicitly allowed.

tabs.label: Ingress
tabs.body:
This is the direction from client to agent. When a request arrives, the gateway forwards it to Model Armor for inspection; if the decision is ALLOW, the request is passed to the agent. If the decision is BLOCK, the client receives an error and the flow terminates.

Responses are also inspected in the same manner before being sent out. You can use the same template for bidirectional traffic, or configure separate templates for each direction.

tabs.label: Egrees
tabs.body: This indicates the direction of communication between an agent and external tools or models. It also monitors traffic within the segment where the agent calls a tool and receives a response. This helps prevent harmful or sensitive content from being mixed into the response and returned to the agent.

tabs.label: Operational efficiency
tabs.body: Filtering logic does not need to be included in the agent code, as the same criteria applies to all agents managed by the gateway. Violations are logged and can be viewed on the Model Armor page and in Security Command Center.

screens.outro: Now, we will compare the gateway filter and the model safety settings side by side and verify the constraints.

screens.title: Distinction between model safety configurations and constraints
screens.lead: Compare how the gateway filter and model safety settings differ in the table. Below the table, the constraints of Model Armor integration are summarized.

data.caption: Comparison between Gateway Filters and Model Safety Settings
rows: The pathway through which requests and responses pass, outside the model
Part of the model call, inside the model
All agents managed by the gateway
Organizational policies unrelated to the model
Settings defined per call, threshold values by hazardous category, etc.

Basic Safety Net, System Guidelines, Harm Type Thresholds, Custom Safety Checks, Block List
data.notes: Gemini Safety Documents describe multiple layers including basic safety controls, system guidelines, hazard-type thresholds, customized safety checks, sensitive information leakage prevention, and blocklists. These approaches are not mutually exclusive but rather overlap to form a multi-layered defense strategy. However, Model Armor integration comes with limitations. Model Armor and its linked services must reside in the same region, and cross-region calls are not supported. Ingress protection is supported only by agents built using ADK, while egress inline protection is limited to MCP server, OpenAI-style services, and A2A integrations. Prompts and responses that include document uploads or file uploads are not sanitized within this integration. When using templates across multiple projects, sufficient API allocation must be available in both projects.

screens.outro: Having verified the comparisons and constraints, let's illustrate how filtering occurs along the path with a concrete example.

screens.title: Explanation: Where is filtering applied in the request and response paths?
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the scenario step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Verify the example
steps.body: An employee asks a corporate document summarization agent a question, and the agent calls internal tools to read the document. Let's follow through this path to see where filtering should be applied.

steps.title: Filters injection and personal information during input validation
steps.body: When an employee's question passes through the gateway, Model Armor checks for prompt injection attempts and personal information. It has not yet reached the agent or the model.

steps.title: Mask or block depending on the decision.
steps.body: If personal information is present, it is masked according to a template and then sent to the model. If a severe violation is detected, it is blocked and an error is returned to the client. The specific response action is defined within the template.

steps.title: Checks the tool call section
steps.body: The agent checks for malicious or sensitive content mixed within tool responses when invoking internal tools, specifically within the ingress. However, since ingress inline protection is limited to certain integrations such as the MCP server, it must first verify whether the target is within its scope. Tool integrations outside the supported range are not subject to this check and therefore require separate mitigation strategies.

steps.title: Checks again before the response returns
steps.body: The response generated by the model is reviewed one final time before being returned to the employee, and is either allowed or blocked. This is because even if the input is clean, sensitive information could potentially be mixed into the output.

steps.title: Records are used for policy improvement.
steps.body: Activated filters remain in the logs and security console. Monitor how frequently each filter triggers and adjust thresholds and templates accordingly. Starting in logging-only mode can help reduce the accidental blocking of normal requests.

screens.outro: Next, we will compare the reasons for keeping filters outside the model.

screens.title: Explanation: Reason for placing a filter outside the model
screens.lead: Compare the difference when the filter is outside the model versus when it is inside the model by alternately selecting between the two states.

states.label: When the filter is placed outside the model
states.body: The policy remains unchanged even if a model is replaced or an agent is added. Since the policy is defined and modified in a single location, changes are fast and control is consistent. During initial deployment, operations can start in a monitoring-only mode to observe the system, and transition to blocking and masking modes if no issues are detected. Templates can be customized per direction, with inputs strictly enforced and outputs focused on sensitive information. Model safety settings remain an effective defensive layer and should be used in conjunction. When two layers overlap, one can compensate for risks that might be missed by the other. The key is not to rely on a single filter.

states.label: When the filter is only inside the model
states.body: Safety controls vary by model and service, leading to decentralized governance. Changing the model may result in different default settings and behaviors for safety configurations, and each new agent requires re-evaluation of these settings. Policies that cannot be easily expressed through model invocation settings—such as prompt injection defenses or organization-specific confidentiality rules—must be implemented separately. As a result, it becomes difficult to determine where and what is filtered from a single centralized view. This also makes it challenging to respond to requests to aggregate and display filtering records during audits or incident investigations. For these reasons, it is recommended to place control authority at key junction points, with model safety settings positioned as an internal, supporting layer.

screens.outro: Now I will summarize the previous content into a single reference point.

screens.title: Summary: Filtering outside the model is advantageous for control.
screens.lead: Summarizing the content discussed so far.

paragraphs: Model Armor examines prompts and responses bidirectionally to detect and block injection, leakage, and harmful content, making allow or block decisions. When integrated with a gateway, the same policy is applied across all agents.

Model safety configurations serve as a multi-layered defense mechanism, overlapping with gateway filters at the call level. However, constraints such as region matching and supported integrations must be verified before implementation. In operations, it is safe to follow the procedure of initially inspecting only for logging and then progressively restricting access to block traffic.

glossary.def: A Google Cloud service that checks prompts and responses to prevent prompt injection, information leakage, and harmful content.
This method checks both the inputs fed into and the outputs produced by the model.
This configuration invokes filters at the entry and exit points of the traffic path to enforce policies.
These are model-level settings that define thresholds by harmful category, etc., during model calls.

misconceptions.fact: Model safety settings are a layer that operates only during that specific call. Separate filter layers need to be placed at gateways for input injection defenses and consistent policies across the entire organization.

misconceptions.myth: Model Armor only performs input validation.
misconceptions.fact: Checks both the prompt and the response. Even if the input is clean, sensitive information could be mixed into the output.

misconceptions.myth: Attaching it to the gateway protects all inputs.
misconceptions.fact: Prompts and responses containing document or file uploads are not sanitized, and constraints specified in the document, such as region matching, must be satisfied.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Filters are advantageous for keeping them outside the model during control.
Model Armor examines both the prompt and the response.
When integrated with the gateway, the same policy is applied across the entire agent.
The gateway filter and model safety settings form a layered defense mechanism used in conjunction.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Where is our filter located, in the request or response path, and does it persist even if the model changes?

checks.q: Want to maintain the same filtering criteria across the entire organization even after adding agents and changing models. What is the most appropriate configuration?
options: Each agent code has its own filtering logic inserted.
Adjust only the threshold values for harmful categories in the model call settings.
At the gateway, it checks requests and responses using the Model Armor template.
Specify prohibited rules in the system guidelines
checks.explain: The gateway filter operates based on organizational policies rather than on any specific model, applying the same criteria to all agents managed by the gateway. Model safety configurations provide a valid defense layer but, as a per-call mechanism, function best when combined with multi-layered defenses.

wrong.0: If each agent has its own separate entry, the baseline becomes inconsistent and may be lost in a new agent.
wrong.1: Model safety settings operate only during that call and the baseline may change when the model changes.
wrong.3: System guidelines are layers that operate within the model and are insufficient for enforcing consistent policies at the organizational level.

checks.q: Place the filters in the order they are applied within the internal document summary agent.
items: Employee queries pass through the gateway and are subject to prompt injection and personal information checks.
Masks personal information according to template and sends it to the model, or blocks it if severe.
The agent checks for harmful or sensitive content in the tool's response during the interval when the agent calls a tool.
The model response is re-evaluated to determine whether it should be ALLOW or BLOCK before being returned to the employee.
The activated filter remains in the logs and security console for policy improvement.
checks.explain: Filters enter at each stage—input, tool calling, output—and their results are recorded as evidence to modify policies.
